Porfirio Díaz. The Mexican military general and statesman who ruled the country for thirty years from 1876 to 1911, bringing modernisation and foreign investment but at the cost of authoritarian control and deep social inequality. His regime's collapse triggered the Mexican Revolution.

Díaz became president through the Plan of Tuxtepec in 1876, establishing the principle of no reelection. Then he violated that principle repeatedly, holding onto power for three decades. The Porfiriato brought railroad expansion, industrialisation, and foreign investment, but it concentrated wealth among a small elite. Díaz suppressed indigenous peoples and campesinos, consolidating land into the hands of large haciendas and foreign corporations. He maintained order through the Rurales, a federal police force used to crush both banditry and political opposition. By 1910, his ageing and apparent indefinite rule triggered the Mexican Revolution when reformer Francisco Madero challenged him. He fled Mexico in May 1911 and died in exile in France in 1915, watching from afar the massive upheaval his own rigidity had sparked. The revolution that overturned his regime would transform Mexico far more radically than he could have imagined, implementing the very agrarian and social reforms that his authoritarian order had denied.
